segments.caption: What if Virat Kohli had played for Pakistan, and Babar Azam for India?
We replayed every ODI they have played since 2015. 10,000 times each.
This is The Swap.
Since May 2015, Kohli averages 65 in ODIs, with 33 hundreds.
Babar averages 52, with 20.
13 more runs every innings for Kohli. And faster.
The gap is widest in a chase.
Batting first, Kohli averages 63. Babar, 56.
Chasing, Kohli climbs to 68. Babar drops to 49.
One gets better. The other gets worse.
Here's the replay. Mohali, 2016. Kohli's 154 not out chases down 286.
Take it out. Drop in a Babar innings, picked at random from his record: chasing, against a top team.
His teammates bat the balls he leaves.
10,000 replays later, India win less than twice in 100.
But first, a fair test.
Each man replaces himself, with a random innings from his own record. That takes the luck out.
India win 101 of 154. Pakistan, 72 of 138.
Now, the swap. India, with Babar at No.3, win 95. About six fewer, more than half of them in chases.
Pakistan, with Kohli, win 76.5. 4.5 more: one extra win every 30 games.
Why not more? Most ODIs aren't close.
Every dot is a match, placed by its winning margin.
Kohli's 13 extra runs mostly matter in this red band. Only 44 of 292 games landed there.
But some nights change.
Colombo, 2023. Pakistan lose to Sri Lanka off the last ball, and miss the Asia Cup final. With Kohli, they win two times in three.
Manchester, 2019. The World Cup semi-final. Kohli makes 1. With Babar, India win one time in five.
And India against Pakistan?
Both men played six of them. India won five. Swap them, and India still win five.
This rivalry was never just about Kohli.
So, the verdict.
Over a decade, Kohli is worth about five more ODI wins than Babar, and the difference lives in the chase.
Swap the shirts, and the gap between the teams narrows. It doesn't close.
Beyond The Scoreboard.
